Four cohort studies involving a total of 28,755 pregnancies were analyzed to evaluate the prognostic properties of the IADPSG diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in predicting large-for-gestational-age (LGA) births. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population who underwent universal screening for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with IADPSG cut-offs. The clinical outcome assessed was the occurrence of LGA births. Data were abstracted from Wendland et al., using a random-effects model and over-dispersion correction. The overall incidence of LGA births was assumed to be 10%. Results were based on the sensitivity and specificity of the diagnostic test. Significant heterogeneity was observed across studies, with better results reported in the HAPO study, where the IADPSG criteria were originally developed. 2. For false negatives, three cohort studies involving 35,902 pregnancies were analyzed. The evidence quality was rated as moderate due to serious inconsistency. The estimated rate of false negatives was 72 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 67–76). 3. For true negatives, the same three cohort studies (35,902 pregnancies) were analyzed. The evidence quality was also rated as moderate due to serious inconsistency. The estimated rate of true negatives was 755 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 734–776). 4. For false positives, the same three cohort studies (35,902 pregnancies) were analyzed. The evidence quality was rated as moderate due to serious inconsistency. The estimated rate of false positives was 145 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 124–166). 5. Complications and costs related to the diagnostic process were not reported in the studies. 6. The prognostic properties of the 1999 WHO diagnostic criteria for GDM in predicting pre-eclampsia were evaluated using three cohort studies involving 26,677 pregnancies. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population who underwent universal screening for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 75g OGTT with WHO cut-offs. The clinical outcome assessed was the development of pre-eclampsia during pregnancy. Data were abstracted from Wendland et al., using a random-effects model and over-dispersion correction. Results were based on the sensitivity and specificity of the diagnostic test. No serious limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision were noted, and the evidence quality was rated as high. 7. For true positives, the estimated rate was 7 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 6–8). For false negatives, the estimated rate was 38 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 37–39). For true negatives, the estimated rate was 860 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 838–880). For false positives, the estimated rate was 95 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 75–117). 8. The prognostic properties of the IADPSG diagnostic criteria for GDM in predicting pre-eclampsia were evaluated using three cohort studies involving 35,052 pregnancies. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population who underwent universal screening for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 75g OGTT with IADPSG cut-offs. The clinical outcome assessed was the development of pre-eclampsia during pregnancy. Data were abstracted from Wendland et al., using a random-effects model and over-dispersion correction. Results were based on the sensitivity and specificity of the diagnostic test. Important heterogeneity was observed across studies, with better results reported in the HAPO study, where the IADPSG criteria were originally developed. 9. For false negatives, the estimated rate was 33 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 32–34). For true negatives, the estimated rate was 796 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 777–816). For false positives, the estimated rate was 159 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 139–178). 10. The prognostic properties of the 1999 WHO diagnostic criteria for GDM in predicting cesarean section were evaluated using four cohort studies involving 30,045 pregnancies. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population who underwent universal screening for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 75g OGTT with WHO cut-offs. The clinical outcome assessed was the occurrence of cesarean section. Data were abstracted from Wendland et al., using a random-effects model and over-dispersion correction. The overall incidence of cesarean section was assumed to be 20%. Results were based on the sensitivity and specificity of the diagnostic test. Most studies lacked blinding for medical staff, and important heterogeneity was observed across studies. 11. For true positives, the estimated rate was 26 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 18–33). For false negatives, the estimated rate was 174 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 167–182). For true negatives, the estimated rate was 715 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 677–754). For false positives, the estimated rate was 85 per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 46–123). 12. The prognostic properties of the IADPSG diagnostic criteria for GDM in predicting cesarean section were evaluated using three cohort studies involving 33,788 pregnancies. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population who underwent universal screening for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation using a 75g OGTT with IADPSG cut-offs. The clinical outcome assessed was the occurrence of cesarean section. Data were abstracted from Wendland et al., using a random-effects model and over-dispersion correction. Important heterogeneity was observed across studies, with better results reported in the HAPO study, where the IADPSG criteria were originally developed. 13. For true positives, the evidence quality was rated as low due to serious inconsistency and indirectness. The estimated rate was 21 fewer per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 8–27). For false negatives, the evidence quality was rated as very low. The estimated rate was 9 fewer per 1,000 tested (95% CI: 5–13). 14. Universal screening for GDM using WHO criteria was compared to no screening in pregnancy. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population. The intervention involved OGTT with specific treatment for women diagnosed with GDM according to WHO criteria. The comparison group received no screening. The outcomes assessed included adverse perinatal and maternal outcomes. The evidence quality was rated as very low due to serious limitations and inconsistency. The absolute effect was highly dependent on GDM prevalence in the model’s sensitivity analysis. 15. Universal screening for GDM using IADPSG criteria was compared to no screening in pregnancy. The population consisted of pregnant women from the general population. The intervention involved OGTT with specific treatment for women diagnosed with GDM according to IADPSG criteria. The comparison group received no screening. The outcomes assessed included adverse perinatal and maternal outcomes. The evidence quality was rated as very low due to serious limitations and inconsistency. The absolute effect was highly dependent on GDM prevalence in the model’s sensitivity analysis.
